analysis.one_liner: Bars accounting firms from selling consulting to companies they audit and requires independent corporate audit committees.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced in the weeks after Enron's collapse, this bill would have stopped accounting firms from earning consulting fees from the same companies they audit, forced auditors off a client after seven straight years, barred auditors from taking executive jobs at their audit clients for a year, and required public companies to disclose financial, professional, and family ties among their directors and executives. It would also have required that the board committees overseeing audits and executive pay be made up solely of independent directors. The bill was read once and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no further action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors — including retirement savers and employees holding company stock through 401(k) plans — benefit from audits they can trust. When an auditor also sells consulting to the same company, it has a business reason to keep that client happy rather than flag problems in the books. Independent audit and compensation committees, and full disclosure of executives' relationships with the company, give investors a clearer picture of who is watching the books and who is setting executive pay.

how_it_helps.text: It bans an accounting firm from providing management consulting or other non-audit services to a company in the same year it audits that company's books, removing a financial tie that can pull an auditor away from honest reporting [S2][S3].

It forces auditors off a client after seven consecutive years and bars an auditor from taking a management or policymaking job at a company it audited within the previous year, breaking up long, comfortable auditor-client relationships [S2][S3].

It requires public companies to disclose the nature, extent, and duration of financial, professional, and family relationships between the company and its directors, executives, and their immediate family members, and requires audit and compensation committees to consist solely of independent directors [S2][S3].
It puts the Senate on record that tough enforcement, including criminal prosecution where possible, is the most effective deterrent to corporate fraud [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large accounting firms lose a lucrative line of business: consulting fees from companies they audit. Public company boards and executives lose flexibility — they must disclose extensive family, professional, and financial relationships and can no longer staff the audit and compensation committees with directors who have ties to management. Some compliance and disclosure costs would flow to public companies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Accounting firms, public companies, and their boards

drawbacks.text: The bill bans essentially all non-audit services, not just the riskiest ones. Critics of blanket bans argue that consulting work can give an auditor useful knowledge about a client's systems, and that a complete split between audit and consulting work raises costs for companies and, indirectly, for their customers and shareholders [S3].

The disclosure requirement reaches every financial, professional, and family relationship 'not more remote than first cousin' for directors and executives, a sweeping rule that companies would have to maintain and that investors would have to wade through [S3].

A hard seven-year rotation limit, with no exception, forces companies to switch auditors even when the relationship is working, with transition costs and no guarantee the new firm starts with the same understanding of the business [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections address a real and proven problem: the 2001-2002 accounting scandals showed that auditors earning large consulting fees from clients sometimes did not press hard on questionable accounting. The blanket ban on all non-audit services and the broad family-relationship disclosure are blunt instruments, and Congress's later accounting reform of 2002 took a narrower route — banning specific risky services rather than everything. On balance the bill's protections for investors outweigh its compliance costs, though it was rougher-edged than the law that eventually passed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2002, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the bill on March 21, 2002, with Sen. Jean Carnahan as the bill's sole cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; that referral is the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill sat in committee for the remaining nine and a half months of the Congress and was never voted on by the committee or the full Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The accounting firms kept their consulting business with audit clients for the rest of the 107th Congress, and public companies kept boards and committees structured as before. Months after this bill stalled, Congress did pass major accounting-reform legislation in 2002 that included auditor-independence rules, so investors ultimately gained much of this ground through a different bill — but this particular bill died without moving.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Accounting firms; later, investors via 2002 reform law

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Integrity in Auditing Act of 2002 and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Paul Sarbanes, D-MD)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 2002 and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Major accounting firms
against.role: Auditors to nearly all large public companies
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed restrictions on selling consulting services to audit clients during the 2002 debate over accounting reform.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record; the bill's only two sponsors were Democrats and the committee that held it was chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill bans consulting and other non-audit services to audit clients, forces a new auditor after seven years, and bars auditors from joining client management for a year — all revenue and relationship advantages the firms would lose. Their fees ultimately come from the companies whose books they must police, which is exactly the conflict the bill targets.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their boards
industries.note: Companies would have to disclose extensive family, professional, and financial ties of directors and executives, and staff audit and compensation committees entirely with independent directors, reducing management's influence over its own watchdogs and pay setting.

industries.industry: Executive recruiting and corporate governance consultants
industries.note: Tighter independence rules and required independent committees would create demand for outside expertise in structuring boards and vetting directors.
